subject: Art & Design
title: Primary Colors: The Unmixable Three
description: A quick win: understand Primary Colors: The Unmixable Three.

hook.text: You can mix orange from red and yellow. But you can't mix red from anything. That's a primary.

buildup.text: In traditional painting, the three primaries are red, yellow, and blue (RYB).

discovery.text: In light (screens), primaries are red, green, and blue — RGB. They combine into white, not brown.

twist.text: Printers use cyan, magenta, and yellow — CMYK. Every color system disagrees on what's primary.

climax.text: The concept of 'primary' depends on the medium. There are no universal primary colors.

punchline.text: Primaries aren't facts of nature. They're tools of the medium.

quiz.question: Why do screens use RGB instead of RYB?

details.summary: Primary colors cannot be created by mixing other colors and serve as the foundation for all other colors. In traditional art, they are red, yellow, and blue (RYB). In light, they are red, green, and blue (RGB). In print, they are cyan, magenta, and yellow (CMY). The model depends on the medium.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding primary colors is understanding the building blocks of all color. Choosing the wrong color model — using paint primaries for screen design, for example — leads to muddy, inaccurate results because each medium mixes color differently.
takeaways: Primary colors cannot be made by mixing other colors
RYB for paint, RGB for screens, CMY for printing
The correct model depends on the medium being used

faq.question: Why are the primary colors different for light and paint?
faq.answer: Paint works by subtractive mixing — pigments absorb light and reflect what's left. Light works by additive mixing — wavelengths combine to create new colors. Different physics require different primaries. Red, green, and blue light combine to white; red, yellow, and blue paint combine to near-black.

faq.question: Are red, yellow, and blue the true primaries for paint?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Modern color science shows that cyan, magenta, and yellow produce a wider range of mixed colors than traditional RYB. Professional printing uses CMY for this reason. RYB persists in art education because it's simpler and historically established.
